strengths: Soundness: The WRITE/READ formulation is clear, and optimizing only prefix-memory tokens with a context-reconstruction loss is technically coherent. The context-removal protocol ensures that answers must pass through the learned memory.

Evidence: The controlled associative-retrieval experiments provide a useful matched comparison: with the same four-layer backbone and eight memory vectors, GradMem substantially outperforms RMT, reaching 99.1% accuracy on 64 pairs with five updates versus 19.3% for one forward RMT update. Results include three-run variability and ablations showing the importance of meta-learning.

Originality and significance: Combining a model-level reconstruction objective, per-context gradient updates, and meta-learning for effective few-step writing is an interesting synthesis. The finding that additional inference-time optimization can improve a fixed memory state is potentially useful for contexts reused across many queries.

Presentation: The method, objectives, and distinction from TTT layers and forward-only memory writers are explained well. The manuscript also candidly discusses second-order training cost, kernel limitations, amortization requirements, and the likely inadequacy of reconstruction for every downstream task.

Reproducibility: The appendix supplies architectures, memory sizes, initialization choices, an inner-learning-rate search range, and implementation/latency details for double backward. The paper also states that source code is supplied.
Ethics: The work presents no obvious direct ethical hazard, uses established benchmarks, and makes no claims involving human subjects or sensitive data.
weaknesses: Soundness and scope: Most compelling evidence comes from a synthetic key-value task with tiny randomly initialized models. Eight 128-dimensional floating-point vectors have ample raw numerical capacity for the reported symbolic data, so these results demonstrate learned access more clearly than meaningful compression under a bit- or byte-matched budget.

The natural-language evidence does not substantiate the paper's broader competitiveness claims. GradMem is markedly worse on bAbI QA3 (79.3–80.0 EM versus 87.9 for RMT, 92.3 for ARMT, and 96.7 for Mamba), its one-step Short SQuAD result is below RMT, ARMT, and Mamba, and its language-modeling cross-entropy of 2.92 is the worst recurrent result. Increasing K helps Short SQuAD but still trails GPT-2 and Mamba, while no increased-K language-modeling result is reported.

The evaluation uses only GPT-2/Pythia/Mamba models around 124–160M parameters, contexts generally no longer than 300 tokens for downstream QA, and an especially simplified Short SQuAD containing only the answer-bearing sentence. This is far from the long-document, codebase, and multi-session applications motivating the work.

Baseline and memory comparisons are not fully controlled. Mamba and ARMT use per-layer states of different forms and sizes, while the principal matched baseline is only RMT. There is no comparison against strong learned context-compression or contemporary test-time-memory methods discussed in related work, and memory is counted as persistent vectors without a byte-matched treatment of precision, added parameters, or WRITE-time activation and gradient storage.

The inference-step scaling protocol is insufficiently specified. Figure 4 reports “best of 0..10/20/30,” but does not explain whether K is selected on validation data or using test exact match; Table 2 likewise says “increased K” without giving the chosen K or selection rule. If selected on test performance, this would constitute test-set tuning; even otherwise, it impedes interpretation and reproduction.

The practical-efficiency case is narrow and underdocumented. GradMem reportedly breaks even with cached GPT-2 only after roughly 64 queries to the same context. The analytical break-even curve does not state the assumed backward/forward cost ratio R, and latency experiments omit important protocol details such as precision, compilation, warm-up, and exact numerical measurements.

Reproducibility is incomplete despite the promised code: the manuscript omits outer-loop optimizer settings, learning rates and schedules, training steps, batch sizes for the main tasks, dataset split/preprocessing details, exact per-experiment inner rates, checkpoint-selection rules, and several baseline-tuning details. Curriculum training and different initialization procedures further complicate controlled replication.

Limitations and ethics: The compute discussion is welcome, but there is no explicit limitations or broader-impact treatment of the substantial training/test-time energy cost, privacy implications of portable context memories, or whether stored continuous memories can leak sensitive source text. These are relevant for the proposed persistent-memory use case.

strengths: Originality: GradMem offers a conceptually clean combination of per-context prefix optimization, a self-supervised reconstruction objective, and meta-learning for few-step writes. This is meaningfully distinct from purely forward RMT-style updates, despite being closely related to prompt optimization, test-time training, and prior iterative embedding compression.

Soundness within a narrow setting: the context-removal formulation is clear, and the controlled associative-retrieval experiments show a large empirical advantage over the particular RMT implementation using the same eight-vector memory state. The evaluation includes three-run variability and demonstrates that additional optimization steps can improve retrieval.

Presentation: the WRITE/READ formulation and inner/outer objectives are generally explained well. The figures make the method understandable, and the appendices discuss second-order differentiation, measured latency, and reconstruction-loss behavior.

Potential significance: a compact state that is expensive to construct once but reusable across many queries could be useful. The paper appropriately acknowledges the substantial training and inference costs and attempts to characterize the amortization regime.
The custom double-backward study appears practically useful, reporting both latency and memory consumption up to 1024 tokens.
weaknesses: Soundness: the central claim that gradient-based writing is superior to forward-only writing is supported primarily by comparison with one RMT writer. The methods are not compute-matched: a gradient update requires a forward and backward pass, while an RMT update is only a forward pass. Comparing equal numbers of updates therefore gives GradMem substantially more computation. Re-reading with the same RMT is not an adequate substitute for stronger or deeper compute-matched encoders, and an unrolled gradient procedure is itself a fixed computation, so the manuscript's broader expressivity language is not established.

The synthetic capacity results are heavily training-specific. Models are curriculum-trained separately for increasing numbers of pairs, the inner learning rate is selected per K using the best setup, failing baselines are not evaluated at larger sizes, and repeated-RMT results contain large instability and many missing entries. This does not establish general capacity scaling of a fixed trained system.

The natural-language evidence is too weak for the claimed transfer and long-context motivation. bAbI is synthetic, Short SQuAD reduces each passage to the answer-containing sentence at roughly 40 tokens, and language modeling writes only 128 tokens. GradMem is worse than RMT or ARMT on important reported settings, including bAbI QA3 and language modeling, while the improved-K result is reported only selectively. No realistic long-document, multi-query benchmark demonstrates that the retained memory remains useful.

The most relevant contemporary alternatives—such as ICAE/SelfCP-style compression, Cartridges, Atlas/Titans, end-to-end TTT, and optimized context-compression methods—are discussed but not experimentally compared. Consequently, the experiments establish an advantage over a limited RMT baseline rather than the state of the art.

Table 2 contains an impossible Short SQuAD exact-match value of 963.3% for Mamba. More broadly, the table mixes different pretrained bases, memory structures, parameter counts, and effective state sizes, so claims such as being competitive across downstream tasks are difficult to interpret.

Reproducibility is inadequate in the manuscript: it omits essential outer-loop optimizer and learning-rate settings, training duration, batch sizes, data splits or sample counts, checkpoint/model-selection rules, decoding details, seeds, and the actual K used for the vaguely labeled 'increased K' rows. The blank code URL in the paper and a general statement that code is supplementary do not resolve these missing experimental specifications.

The efficiency analysis rests on a simplified quadratic-attention model that ignores dominant projection/MLP costs in the tested length regime. Figure 6 does not state the assumed update-cost ratio R or K, and the latency study does not report enough implementation and measurement detail to validate fairness. The observed break-even point of roughly 64 repeated reads also indicates a specialized deployment regime, not broad efficiency.

Important ablations are absent: learned initialization, memory projections, separate WRITE/READ heads, reconstruction versus alternative inner losses, first-order meta-learning, memory size, precision, and compute-matched alternatives are not isolated. The row called 'without meta-learning' is also described as a first-order approximation, conflating distinct interventions.

The paper discusses computational limitations honestly, which should not itself be penalized, and the work presents no obvious direct societal-risk issue. However, it does not quantify training cost or energy despite relying on costly second-order optimization. Overall, the narrow synthetic evidence does not support the central comparative and practical claims strongly enough for acceptance.

strengths: The method is technically coherent: GradMem optimizes only a compact prefix memory at test time using an explicit reconstruction loss, while meta-training differentiates through the write steps. The context-removal protocol ensures that reported retrieval cannot directly use the original context.

The controlled associative-retrieval experiment provides strong evidence for the core mechanism. With the same 8-vector memory and base architecture, GradMem substantially outperforms RMT; five gradient updates achieve 88.4% accuracy on 96 pairs versus 12.9% for one forward-only RMT write. Means and standard deviations over three runs are reported.

The evaluation usefully studies test-time scaling beyond the trained number of write steps. The accompanying inner-loss analysis offers a plausible explanation for improved retrieval, particularly through better reconstruction of value tokens.

The paper goes beyond synthetic retrieval with bAbI, Short SQuAD, WikiText-103, analytical break-even calculations, and measured A100 latency. The explicit context-removal setup and empirical latency measurements make the proposed use case unusually concrete.

Presentation is generally clear and well organized. Equations precisely specify the inner and outer objectives, appendices discuss implementation and double-backward costs, and the paper candidly acknowledges substantial training and inference overhead, kernel limitations, and the possible inadequacy of reconstruction for some tasks. Direct ethical risks appear limited.
weaknesses: Evidence for broad practical significance is preliminary. The natural-language evaluation uses toy bAbI tasks, an artificially shortened SQuAD variant with roughly 40-token contexts, and 128-token language-modeling contexts, rather than the genuinely long documents motivating the work.

Natural-language results are mixed. GradMem is much worse on bAbI QA3 than RMT, ARMT, and Mamba; it is the weakest reported recurrent method on WikiText cross-entropy; and increasing K slightly degrades QA2 and QA3. Its strongest natural-language gain is on Short SQuAD, where it still trails GPT-2 and Mamba. Thus the broad claim that performance scales well with K is supported mainly by synthetic retrieval and Short SQuAD.

The main matched comparison controls memory size but not write-time computation. A gradient step requires forward and backward computation, so comparing K gradient steps with K repeated forward passes does not establish superiority at equal FLOPs or latency. Compute-matched learned encoders and more direct recent context-compression or test-time-memory methods are discussed but not empirically compared.

The phrase “task-agnostic” applies only to the inner reconstruction loss. Model parameters and the memory initialization are separately meta-trained using each downstream task loss, and the value-selective behavior in the retrieval analysis can arise through that supervision. No cross-task transfer experiment shows that a trained writer or memory initialization generalizes to a new downstream task.

Reproducibility is only moderate despite the claimed supplementary code. The manuscript omits many concrete training details such as optimizer schedules, batch sizes, training duration, data splits and sample counts. “Increased K” is not numerically specified in Table 2, and the best inner learning rate is selected separately for each synthetic K without a fully described validation protocol.

The compute analysis relies on simplified asymptotic assumptions, while the latency experiment reports no uncertainty, detailed kernel configuration, or equal-quality comparison. Breaking even only after approximately 64 reads for 256–1024-token contexts substantially narrows the practical regime.

Originality is meaningful but moderate: the contribution is a well-executed combination of test-time embedding optimization, meta-learning, prefix memory, and reconstruction, rather than a fundamentally new learning principle. Overall, the compelling synthetic result supports weak acceptance, but the limited and mixed natural-language evidence prevents a stronger rating.

strengths: The core method is clear and technically coherent: context-specific prefix memory is optimized using a model-level reconstruction loss, while an outer task loss meta-learns the initialization and model through the unrolled WRITE steps.

The controlled associative-retrieval experiments provide strong evidence for the narrow central result. With the same 8-vector memory as RMT, GradMem substantially improves as WRITE steps increase, reaching 99.1% exact match on 64 pairs at K=5 versus 19.3% for one-pass RMT.

The paper includes useful ablations and analyses: first- versus second-order meta-learning, memory size versus WRITE steps, input-level versus per-layer memory, inner-loss behavior, state-matched Mamba experiments, and comparisons with TTT-Linear and LaCT.

Evaluation reports three-run means and standard deviations, and the empirical latency analysis identifies concrete amortization regimes rather than presenting compressed memory as unconditionally efficient.

The presentation is generally clear, with a well-defined WRITE/READ formulation, algorithm, implementation sketch, and an honest discussion of second-order training and test-time compute costs. No major ethical concern is apparent for the studied tasks.
weaknesses: Evidence beyond synthetic retrieval is not yet convincing. GradMem is worse than ARMT or Mamba on the challenging bAbI QA3 task, roughly tied with RMT on language modeling, and its main natural-language gain is on a specially shortened SQuAD variant whose context is only the answer-containing sentence. This does not establish usefulness for realistic long, distractor-rich contexts.

The broad conclusion that gradient writing is stronger than forward-only writing is supported mainly against RMT. Re-reading the same segment is a weak way to allocate additional compute to RMT, and no compute-matched learned iterative encoder is evaluated. Moreover, an unrolled gradient update is itself a fixed computation, so the claim that it is generally more expressive than forward computation is overstated.

Comparisons conflate memory, compute, architecture, and pretraining. GradMem K=5 uses multiple full-model backward passes, whereas several baselines use one forward update; Mamba, ARMT, TTT, and LaCT have different state sizes and parameterizations. The appendix partially addresses state size, but there is no systematic quality-versus-WRITE-latency or FLOP-matched comparison.

The claimed 16–32x compression for the Llama reconstruction experiment is based on counting input tokens versus dense memory vectors, not bytes, bits, or comparable KV-state storage. Since each vector contains thousands of floating-point values, this ratio is not a meaningful storage-compression measurement without a precision-aware accounting.

Reproducibility is inadequate in the submitted manuscript: both occurrences of “Code is available at” lack a URL, and important details such as outer-loop learning rates, batch sizes, training duration, selection protocol, dataset sizes/splits, prompt formatting, and complete checkpoint construction are absent. Selecting the best inner learning rate separately for each K also needs a specified validation protocol.

Some analyses overinterpret correlation. Lower reconstruction loss and higher retrieval accuracy across WRITE iterations do not establish that improved context retention causes the task gain, and the assertion that memory selectively retains values is not fully supported when keys may already be predictable or represented in ways not measured by token reconstruction loss.

The efficiency model counts attention's quadratic term but omits substantial projection and MLP costs, limiting its predictive validity. Empirical break-even points are often tens of repeated queries, so applicability is restricted to heavily reused contexts.

Presentation has smaller quality issues, including an apparent impossible “963.3%” Mamba score in Table 2 and underspecified “increased K” results. Privacy or leakage risks of storing source content in portable continuous memories are also not discussed.

Overall, the synthetic results and method are promising and original as a particular combination of prompt-memory optimization and meta-learning, but the weak realistic evaluation, incomplete matched comparisons, and reproducibility gaps prevent reliable acceptance in the current form.

strengths: The paper presents a clear and technically interesting formulation: context is written into a fixed-size prefix memory by a few gradient steps on an autoregressive reconstruction loss, while the base model remains frozen during test-time writing.

The controlled associative-retrieval experiments provide credible evidence that the proposed update can work. With eight memory vectors, GradMem substantially outperforms the matched RMT baseline, and performance generally improves with additional gradient steps.

The authors include useful ablations on the number and placement of memory vectors, second-order meta-learning, test-time step extrapolation, and reconstruction loss. Reporting means and standard deviations over three runs is also helpful.

The paper openly discusses the substantial training and inference costs of full-model backpropagation, provides latency measurements, and introduces an implementation for more efficient double backward through attention.

The manuscript is generally well organized, clearly separates WRITE and READ phases, and provides equations, pseudocode, and a reasonably broad discussion of related test-time-training methods. No material research-ethics concern is apparent for the evaluated tasks.
weaknesses: The natural-language evidence does not substantiate the paper's broad motivation around long contexts. The main evaluations use approximately 20–300-token bAbI inputs, an artificially shortened SQuAD containing only the answer-bearing sentence (approximately 40 tokens), and 128 tokens of written context for language modeling. Larger-model reconstruction reaches only 32–64 tokens. None demonstrates useful compression of realistic long documents.

Results beyond the synthetic task are weak or mixed. GradMem is worse than ARMT on the difficult bAbI QA3 task, is essentially tied with RMT in language modeling, and substantially trails full-context models on Short SQuAD. Increasing K hurts or fails to improve several bAbI results. Describing this as successful transfer or competitive long-context performance is therefore overstated.

The favorable long-context latency results are disconnected from task quality: the paper measures writing and reading latency at 4K–16K tokens but provides no retrieval, QA, reconstruction, or language-modeling accuracy for memories written from contexts of those lengths. A fast compressed READ is not useful if the memory has lost the required information, so these measurements do not establish practical efficiency.

Comparisons are not compute matched. One GradMem update requires a full forward and backward pass, whereas the principal RMT baseline uses a forward pass; K=5 multiplies this disparity. Re-reading the identical segment with RMT is also a narrow and potentially poorly suited forward-only comparator. There is no accuracy-versus-latency/FLOP frontier against trained compression methods such as ICAE, SelfCP, or KV-compression approaches.

Claims that the WRITE mechanism is task-agnostic need qualification. Although its inner reconstruction loss is generic, the base-model parameters, memory initialization, projections, and sometimes separate WRITE head are meta-trained using the downstream task loss. Models are trained separately across tasks and synthetic context lengths, so the learned writer has substantial task-specific supervision.

The synthetic capacity experiments train or curriculum-fine-tune models for the evaluated number of key–value pairs. They therefore show in-distribution storage after task-specific training, not robust length generalization. The central 96-pair result also concerns a highly regular random-symbol format and does not establish capacity on natural text.

Reproducibility is inadequate. The claimed code link is blank, and the appendix omits important details such as outer-loop optimizer settings, learning-rate schedules, batch sizes, training duration, dataset split sizes, checkpoint-selection rules, and exact preprocessing. Hyperparameter selection is partly described as reporting the best setting, but the selection protocol is unspecified. The custom double-backward implementation cannot be reconstructed from the minimal pseudocode.

The computational analysis omits important model costs and does not specify all quantities needed to reproduce Figure 6, notably the update-to-forward cost ratio R. Break-even conclusions depend strongly on implementation, answer length, batching, and quality at the chosen compression ratio.

Only three runs are used despite pronounced instability in several baselines, with extremely large standard deviations. Reporting the best LaCT run is especially uninformative without a comparable selection treatment for all methods. Table 2 also appears to contain an impossible SQuAD EM value of 963.3%, indicating insufficient presentation checking.

Overall, the core idea and synthetic proof of concept have merit, but important evidential, fairness, and reproducibility gaps prevent the central claims about practical, transferable, and efficient context memory from being reliable enough for acceptance.

strengths: Soundness: The WRITE/READ formulation is precise: memory tokens are optimized with a context-reconstruction loss, the original context is removed during READ, and the outer task loss is differentiated through the inner updates. The synthetic results strongly support the central feasibility claim: with eight memory vectors, GradMem improves from 86.9% to 99.9% exact match on 32 key-value pairs when increasing from one to five updates, substantially exceeding the matched RMT baseline.

Soundness: The paper includes useful ablations and diagnostics, including removal of second-order meta-learning, memory-size versus WRITE-step sweeps, extrapolation to additional test-time steps, correlations between reconstruction loss and retrieval accuracy, state-size-controlled Mamba comparisons, and input-level versus per-layer memory.

Significance: Compact, reusable context representations are practically relevant. The explicit compute-quality trade-off is valuable, and measured latency results appropriately identify the many-query regime in which the expensive WRITE operation can be amortized.

Originality: Optimizing a small, model-level prefix memory through a few meta-learned gradient steps is a distinctive and conceptually clean combination of test-time training, prompt optimization, and compressive memory. The separation from per-layer online TTT states is clearly articulated.

Presentation: The manuscript is generally clear and well organized. Equations, the minimal algorithm, memory-state accounting, and the candid discussion of higher-order differentiation costs make the method easy to understand.

Reproducibility and ethics: The appendix provides architecture and memory dimensions, inner learning rates, curricula, an implementation sketch, and hardware-level efficiency measurements. The method presents no unresolved material ethical concern, and its substantial compute limitations are discussed honestly.
weaknesses: Soundness: The main comparison does not isolate gradient-based writing from the quality and compute of the encoder strongly enough. RMT is only a one-pass segment writer, and repeated passes simply replace its memory; a learned residual/iterative forward writer or encoder matched for WRITE FLOPs and trainable parameters would be a more decisive control. Thus, the broad claim that gradient writing is more expressive than forward computation is stronger than the evidence.

Soundness and significance: Evidence on realistic long-context use is limited. The strongest quality results are on synthetic retrieval. Short SQuAD uses only the answer-containing sentence (about 40 tokens), while GradMem is worse than ARMT on bAbI QA3 and essentially ties RMT on WikiText language modeling. The 1B–3B experiments test reconstruction of only 8–64 tokens, whereas the 4k–16k experiments report latency without downstream accuracy or retention quality.

Soundness: The memory writer is meta-trained separately using each downstream task loss. Consequently, the inner reconstruction objective is task-agnostic, but the learned model and memory dynamics are not. The wording about transfer could more clearly distinguish transfer of the optimization recipe from zero-shot transfer of a trained memory mechanism.

Significance: The reported state compression counts floating-point memory entries rather than information capacity, and the synthetic random key-value contexts contain far fewer bits than suggested by token-count or KV-cache ratios. Claims about memory capacity and compression should therefore be qualified.

Reproducibility: Despite stating that code is available, the manuscript contains no visible URL. Important details such as outer-loop optimizer settings, training duration, model-selection protocol, dataset sizes/splits, preprocessing, decoding, and the complete hyperparameter search are also missing. Selecting the best inner learning rate separately for each K further requires a clearly specified validation protocol.

Presentation: Table 2 appears to report an impossible 963.3% Short-SQuAD exact-match score for Mamba, presumably a typo for 63.3%. Several comparisons use materially different state sizes and initializations, and although these are disclosed, they make the headline tables harder to interpret.

Ethics and limitations: The impact statement is boilerplate. A portable memory explicitly trained to retain context raises plausible privacy, extraction, and sensitive-data persistence risks that deserve brief discussion, even though they do not presently constitute a material barrier to acceptance.
